The work itself is the offering, and God is not honored by an offering thrown together carelessly. This does not mean every Christian must be the best in their field, which is impossible, but it does mean the Christian brings a particular integrity to their labor, a refusal to do bad work, because the work is being done, at the deepest level, unto the Lord. The competence of a believer's work is part of their witness, and often a louder part than their words.

Work and the Body of Christ

There is a final dimension that the individualism of modern work culture obscures: work is meant to be woven into a body, not performed in isolation. The New Testament's vision of the church as a body with many members, each contributing a different function, is fundamentally a vision of interdependent labor. No member does everything; each does their part; and the whole depends on all the parts working together. This is a picture of work as it was meant to be — diverse callings, mutually dependent, contributing to a common good larger than any individual.

Our economy has largely stripped this out, atomizing work into isolated individual careers pursued for individual advancement. But the Christian recovers the truth that their work is part of something larger, that they labor not merely for themselves but as one member serving the whole, that the electrician and the teacher and the nurse and the farmer are all doing their part in a vast web of interdependent service through which God provides for his world. This is dignifying and humbling at once: dignifying, because your work matters to the whole; humbling, because you are not the whole, only a member, and the body does not depend on you alone. To work as a member of the body is to work without the crushing burden of self-importance and without the diminishment of self-contempt, taking your place in a larger service that God is orchestrating.

So work. Work hard, work well, work as the way God loves the person on the other end of your labor. But do not make work your identity, because it is not strong enough to hold you. Work is worship when it is offered to God and rest when it is surrendered to God, and both are needed, and the one who cannot rest has not yet understood who is actually running the world.

chapters.title: What Is Vocation? Work as Calling
chapters.summary: Vocation is not the job that makes you feel important, it is the place where God hides himself behind your ordinary work to feed your neighbor.
chapters.body:
A woman stands at a sink at six in the morning, washing the same dishes she washed last night, and somewhere underneath the steam she is wondering whether any of this counts. She is not lazy. She is not faithless. She has simply absorbed, the way we all absorb the air, a quiet verdict that the real work of God happens somewhere else, in a pulpit or a mission field or a worship band, and that what she does with her two hands at this sink is the part of life you get through so the meaningful part can begin.

I have stood near that sink. I have watched men in my church carry the same suspicion into the cab of a truck, into a classroom, into a cubicle they cannot wait to leave. The question is older than they know, and it is not really a question about jobs. It is a question about whether the eight or ten hours that swallow most of our waking lives have any weight in front of God, or whether they are simply the toll we pay for the privilege of being alive.

The word we reach for is vocation. We have nearly ruined it. In common speech a vocation has become a fancy synonym for a career you happen to enjoy, the work that expresses your inner self, the thing you would do for free if money were no object. That definition sounds generous and it is actually cruel, because it quietly tells the woman at the sink and the man in the truck that they have no vocation at all. Only the lucky few who love their labor get to call it holy. Everyone else is just working.

Let me state the strongest version of the secular objection, because it deserves to be heard plainly. The honest skeptic says this. Calling is a comforting story religion tells to dignify drudgery. There is no cosmic assignment behind your spreadsheet. Work is the exchange of effort for survival, and dressing it in the language of divine purpose is a way of keeping people content with arrangements that mostly serve someone else. He is not entirely wrong. A great deal of vocation talk has functioned exactly that way, a sedative handed to the tired so they will not ask who profits from their tiredness. If your doctrine of work cannot account for the worker who is being ground down, it is not a doctrine. It is propaganda.

So I will not answer the soft version. I will answer that one.

The text I want to carry is the oldest one we have about work, and it falls before anything has gone wrong. 'The Lord God took the man and put him in the garden of Eden to work it and keep it' (Genesis 2:15 ESV). Read that slowly. The garden is unfallen. There is no curse, no sweat, no thorn. And there is already a job. Before the man is given a wife, before there is a single commandment about good and evil, he is given labor. Work is not the punishment that arrived when paradise broke. Work was in paradise. It is part of what it means to bear the image of a God who himself worked six days and called the result good.

This changes the ground under everything. If work belongs to creation rather than to the fall, then the curse in Genesis 3 did not invent labor, it poisoned labor that already existed. The thorns and the sweat are the corruption of a good thing, not the thing itself. Which means redemption does not rescue us from work. It rescues work.

Martin Luther saw this with a clarity the medieval church had lost. The church of his day had built a two story house. Upstairs lived the priests, the monks, the nuns, the people with a vocatio, a true calling. Downstairs lived the farmer and the cobbler and the mother, doing necessary but spiritually second class things while they waited for Sunday. Luther took an axe to the staircase. He insisted that the milkmaid pouring milk and the monk at prayer stood on level ground before God, that the German word Beruf, calling, belonged to the plowman as fully as to the preacher (Luther). I will treat his argument lightly here, because it has been told elsewhere, but the core of it must stand. There is no hierarchy of holy occupations. There is only faithful and unfaithful labor.

Dorothy Sayers pressed the point into the twentieth century with a sentence that still indicts most of our preaching. She wrote that the church has never quite known what to do with work, that we tell the carpenter not to get drunk and not to cheat his customers, and then we fall silent, when the real Christian question is whether he is making good tables (Sayers 1942). A good table, made well, is not a neutral act that becomes holy only if the carpenter slips a tract into the drawer. The goodness of the table is the worship. God is not impressed by shoddy work done in his name. He is honored by sound work, whether or not the worker can name him yet.

Here is where vocation becomes something other than self expression. Lester DeKoster gave the cleanest definition I have found. Work, he wrote, is the form in which we make ourselves useful to others, and therefore the way we love our neighbor in the most concrete terms available to us (DeKoster 1982). Pull the thread. The farmer does not eat most of what he grows. The nurse does not heal herself. The woman at the sink is feeding people who did not earn the meal. Strip the whole economy down to its bones and you find millions of people serving strangers they will never meet, and the serving is so woven into the ordinary that nobody notices it is love.

Luther had a startling phrase for this. He said that God milks the cows through the milkmaid, that the hands of the laborer are the hands God uses to answer the prayer give us this day our daily bread. You pray for bread. God does not drop loaves from the sky. He feeds you through a farmer, a miller, a baker, a trucker, a clerk, a chain of human hands most of whom have no idea they are participating in an answered prayer. Vocation is the mask of God. He hides behind your ordinary work and uses it to keep his world alive.

Now return to the skeptic, who was right that calling has been used as a sedative. He was right, and the answer is not to abandon vocation but to recover the half of it the sedative left out. Because if my work is genuinely the place where God loves my neighbor through my hands, then any arrangement that crushes the worker or empties the work of its service is not a neutral economic fact. It is a violation of something sacred. The doctrine that dignifies the laborer is the same doctrine that condemns his exploitation. You cannot hold one without the other. The factory that treats a man as a disposable input is not merely inefficient. It is desecrating an image bearer at the exact point where he was made to reflect God most clearly.

Studs Terkel spent years recording how Americans actually talk about their jobs, and the ache that runs through his pages is not that the work is hard. It is that the work feels meaningless, that people suspect they are interchangeable, that nobody would notice if they vanished (Terkel 1974). That ache is theological before it is economic. It is the cry of people made for vocation and handed only employment.

So what is vocation. It is not the career that flatters you. It is not the passion you would chase if the bills disappeared. It is the ordinary labor, paid or unpaid, glamorous or invisible, through which God serves your neighbor while wearing you as his mask. The woman at the sink is not waiting for her real calling. Her hands are full of it. The dishes she is washing will hold the food that feeds the people God gave her, and the steam rising off the water is closer to incense than she has been told.

The man who wants only to feel important will never see this, because importance is exactly the wrong measure. The kingdom does not run on importance. It runs on service that mostly goes unwatched. And the test of whether you have understood your vocation is not whether it makes you feel significant. It is whether, when you set down your tools tonight, someone you may never meet was quietly fed.

That is the calling. It was here before the fall. It will outlast your ambition.

### Works Cited

DeKoster, Lester. Work the Meaning of Your Life. Grand Rapids: Christian's Library Press, 1982.

Luther, Martin. The Estate of Marriage and selected writings on vocation. In Luther's Works. Philadelphia: Fortress Press.

Sayers, Dorothy L. Why Work? London: Methuen, 1942.

Terkel, Studs. Working. New York: Pantheon Books, 1974.

chapters.title: When You Hate Your Job
chapters.summary: Much Christian teaching on work speaks to those who love it or can leave it. But most people cannot quit, and many do not love what they do. The gospel has something to say to the trapped and the weary.
chapters.body:
A great deal of Christian writing about work assumes a reader with options. It talks about finding your calling, pursuing your passion, aligning your gifts with your labor, and it presumes that if you are unhappy in your work you can simply find something better. This is advice for the fortunate. It is written for people with education, mobility, savings, and choices. And it has almost nothing to say to the vast number of people who hate their jobs and cannot leave them — the ones supporting families on work they despise, trapped by circumstance in labor that drains them, going back on Monday to something they dread because the alternative is not having a job at all.

I want to write to that person, because they are more common than the Christian bookstore suggests, and because the honest truth is that most human work throughout history has not been fulfilling. The peasant did not love the field. The factory worker did not find their passion on the line. The idea that work should be personally meaningful is a modern, affluent expectation, and holding it up as the standard leaves the majority feeling like spiritual failures for not enjoying labor that was never designed to be enjoyed. There is a better word than that, and it comes from the Scriptures themselves.

The Curse Is Real

Begin with honesty about the source of the misery, because the Bible is more honest about it than most Christian encouragement. When Adam and Eve fell, part of the curse fell specifically on work. "Cursed is the ground because of you; through painful toil you will eat food from it all the days of your life. It will produce thorns and thistles for you. By the sweat of your brow you will eat your food." Work, which was good, became frustrating, futile, and hard. The thorns are not a metaphor. They are the built-in resistance of a broken world to human effort — the projects that fail, the labor that goes unrewarded, the toil that produces exhaustion more than satisfaction.

This means that if you hate your job, you are not necessarily doing anything wrong, and you are certainly not alone in the human story. The frustration of work is a feature of the fallen world, experienced by nearly everyone who has ever labored. The Bible does not promise that faithful people will love their work. It tells the truth: that work east of Eden involves thorns, and that the sweat and the futility are part of the deal for all of us. Naming this is itself a mercy, because it releases you from the false guilt of thinking your misery is a personal spiritual failure. It is the human condition, and Scripture says so plainly.

The Bible never promised you would love your work. It promised thorns. If you hate your job, you are not a bad Christian. You are a laborer in a cursed field, like nearly everyone who has ever worked.

Working as Unto the Lord

The most powerful word for the person trapped in hated work comes from Paul, and it was written to actual slaves — people in a condition of forced labor far worse than any modern job. "Whatever you do, work at it with all your heart, as working for the Lord, not for human masters, since you know that you will receive an inheritance from the Lord as a reward." Slaves. Working for masters who owned them, in conditions they did not choose and could not leave. And Paul tells them their labor can be offered to Christ, seen by Christ, and rewarded by Christ — regardless of the injustice of their situation or the character of their earthly master.

This is transformative for the person who hates their job, and I want to be careful not to make it into a cheap slogan, because Paul was not offering a slogan to slaves. He was offering a genuine reframe. Your real employer is not the company you resent. Your real employer is God, and God sees the work you do even when your earthly boss does not, even when the work is thankless, even when no one notices whether you do it well or badly. The excellence you bring to hated work is not for the company. It is an offering to God, seen and treasured by him. This does not make the job enjoyable. It gives it a dignity the job itself could never provide.

Providing as Love

There is a second reframe that reaches the person supporting a family on work they despise, and it is this: the work you hate is an act of love for the people you are providing for. The father who drags himself to a job he dreads so his children can eat is not merely enduring; he is loving. The mother working a shift she hates so the rent gets paid is pouring herself out for the ones who depend on her. Paul says that anyone who does not provide for their household has denied the faith. Providing is not a lesser calling than passion. It is love made concrete in labor, and there is something in it closer to the cross than any dream job could offer.

This matters because it locates the meaning of the hated work not in the work itself but in the people it serves. You may find no meaning in the task. You may find enormous meaning in the fact that this task keeps your children fed and housed and clothed. The meaning was never supposed to come from the labor alone; it comes from the love the labor serves. When you understand that your despised job is the vehicle of your love for your family, the job does not become enjoyable, but it becomes bearable in a different way — not as pointless suffering but as costly love.

Honest About the Limits

I do not want to spiritualize away real problems, so let me be honest about the limits of these reframes. Some jobs are genuinely destructive — abusive, exploitative, degrading in ways that damage the soul. The call to work as unto the Lord is not a call to remain forever in situations that are crushing you, if there is any way out. Paul told slaves to work faithfully, but he also told them that if they could gain their freedom, they should. Contentment in hard circumstances is not the same as passivity in the face of injustice, and the person in a genuinely toxic situation should seek to change it if they possibly can. Faithfulness in a hated job is not the same as resignation to abuse.

And even in a job that is merely unpleasant rather than destructive, it is right to seek better if the door opens. Nothing in Scripture requires you to stay miserable when you could serve God and your family more fully elsewhere. The reframes are not meant to keep you trapped. They are meant for the person who, right now, cannot leave — to give them a way to live faithfully in the meantime, whatever the meantime turns out to be.

The Weight and the Hope

The Small Redemptions

Even in work you hate, there are usually small openings for meaning that the theology of neighbor-love can help you find, and they are worth naming because they can make the unbearable bearable. You may despise the job itself, but there are people around you — coworkers, customers, the person at the next station — and the way you treat them is not dictated by the job. You can bring dignity, kindness, and honesty into a workplace that has none of these, and in doing so you become a small mercy in someone else's hard day. The job may be meaningless; the way you do it never is.

I have known people who transformed their experience of hated work not by changing the work but by changing what they paid attention to. The security guard who decided to genuinely see and greet every person who passed his desk. The clerk who made it her mission to be the one kind interaction in her customers' frustrating errands. The factory worker who quietly looked out for the new hires no one else helped. They did not love their jobs any more than before, but they found within the jobs a field for love, and the love gave the drudgery a meaning the task itself could never supply. This is the neighbor-love theology applied at the most practical level: even where the work is empty, the neighbor is not, and the neighbor is always an opportunity to serve the God you cannot serve through the task.

Holding On to the Ending

Finally, the person trapped in hated work needs the long view that Scripture provides, because the misery feels endless when you are inside it, and the endlessness is part of what crushes. But it is not endless. The curse on work is not the final word; it is a temporary condition of a world in the process of being redeemed. The same Bible that describes the thorns and thistles promises a day when the creation itself will be liberated from its bondage to decay, when the futility that groans through all our labor will be lifted, when work will become again what it was in the garden before the fall — pure joy, pure fruitfulness, labor without frustration in the presence of God.

This is not escapism; it does not tell you to endure now because it will all be over later and nothing you do in the meantime matters. It tells you the opposite: that your faithful labor now, offered to God in the cursed field, is connected to that coming restoration, that you are not merely surviving until the end but participating, however dimly, in a redemption that is already underway and will one day be complete. The thorns are real, and one day they will be gone.

The Difference Between Hating and Being Destroyed

I want to draw a careful line, because there is a difference between a job you hate and a job that is destroying you, and the counsel differs for each. A job you merely hate — that is boring, thankless, beneath your abilities, or simply unpleasant — is a job you can endure faithfully, offering the drudgery to God and finding meaning in the love it serves. Most hated jobs are of this kind, and the reframes of faithfulness and provision apply directly to them. You can be miserable in such a job and still be spiritually whole, still be faithful, still be growing.

But some jobs cross a line into genuine destruction. The workplace that is abusive, that demands you compromise your integrity, that crushes your spirit so relentlessly that it is deforming your character and your relationships and your faith, is not a job to be nobly endured indefinitely. There is a point at which faithfulness means seeking a way out rather than staying put, at which remaining is not endurance but self-destruction. Discerning the difference requires wisdom and often the counsel of others who can see what you cannot, because the person inside a destructive job often loses the ability to judge how bad it has become. If your work is not merely making you unhappy but genuinely damaging your soul, the call to work as unto the Lord does not require you to stay. It may, in fact, require you to leave.

The God Who Was a Worker

The final comfort for the person who hates their work is that the God they serve is not a stranger to hard labor. Jesus worked as a carpenter for most of his adult life, in a trade that involved real physical toil, in an obscure town, doing ordinary work that no one recorded and no one celebrated. The Son of God spent the majority of his earthly years not preaching to crowds but working with his hands in a village workshop, and there is no indication that the work was easy or the days were exciting. He knows what it is to labor in obscurity, to do work that goes unnoticed, to feel the sweat and the weariness of ordinary toil in a fallen world.

This means the God you cry out to from your hated job is not distant from your experience but has shared it. He is not a deity who only knows the mountaintops of ministry; he knew the long grind of daily work, and he sanctified it by doing it faithfully himself. When you drag yourself back to the job you dread, you are not alone, and you are not doing something beneath the notice of God. You are doing something the Son of God himself did for years, and he sees you, and he understands, in a way no one who has not labored could understand. The carpenter from Nazareth is with you in the cursed field, because he worked it too.

So to the person who will go back on Monday to work they dread: your misery is real, and it is not a sign of spiritual failure. It is the shape of labor in a fallen world, shared by nearly everyone. But your work is seen by a God who misses nothing, offered to a Lord who will reward it, and poured out in love for people who depend on you. Until the day the thorns are gone, you work in the cursed field like the rest of us, faithfully, as unto the Lord, in love for those you carry. That is not nothing. In the eyes of heaven, it may be everything.

chapters.title: When Your Vocation Is Your Calling
chapters.summary: The language of calling has been cheapened into a self-help slogan about finding your passion. Recovering its theological weight changes both the fortunate who love their work and the many who do not.
chapters.body:
The word calling has fallen on hard times. It has been absorbed into the vocabulary of the personal-brand economy, where it means something like the intersection of your passion and your talent, the work you were born to do, the thing that makes you come alive. Find your calling, we tell young people, as though the goal of life were self-actualization through employment. And so calling has become a source of anxiety for the many who do not feel any such thing about their jobs, and a source of quiet self-congratulation for the few who do.

The Christian doctrine of vocation is both richer and stranger than this. The word vocation comes from the Latin vocare, to call, and it presupposes a caller. You cannot be called by an impersonal universe or a career aptitude test. Calling requires a voice, and the doctrine of vocation locates that voice in God. This single fact reorients the entire conversation. The question is not what do I want to do with my life but what is God calling me to do — and the difference between those two questions is the difference between a slogan and a theology.

The Primary Calling

Os Guinness, in his book The Call, makes a distinction that clears away most of the confusion. There is a primary calling and there are secondary callings, and we get into trouble when we collapse the two. The primary calling — the one that is true of every Christian without exception — is the call to God himself. You are called first not to a task but to a person. "Come to me," Jesus says. The primary calling is to belong to Christ, to follow him, to be his. Everything else is downstream of that.

The secondary callings are the particular tasks, roles, relationships, and works to which God directs each person: this marriage, this job, this neighborhood, this responsibility. These are real callings, but they are secondary, and the moment we invert the order — the moment the job becomes the primary calling and God becomes the resource that helps us succeed at it — we have committed a fundamental idolatry, and we will suffer for it. The person whose identity is fused with their work will be destroyed when the work is taken away, because they have made a secondary thing carry a primary weight.

You are not called to a job. You are called to a Person, and then sent into a job. Reverse those and the job will eventually consume you, because it was never strong enough to be first.

The Gift and the Danger of Loving Your Work

Let me speak to the fortunate first, because they need a warning that the culture will never give them. If you love your work — if it fits your gifts, engages your mind, serves your neighbor, and pays your bills — that is a genuine grace, and you should receive it with gratitude. Not everyone gets it. To have work that feels like calling is a gift, and gifts are meant to be enjoyed.

But the gift carries a specific danger, and it is precisely the danger of the fortunate: the work becomes the identity. When your job is your calling in the deepest sense, when it is where you find meaning and worth and purpose, it is terrifyingly easy for it to displace God as the center of your life. You will pray about your work, tithe from your work, thank God for your work, and never notice that the work has become your functional god and the actual God has become its assistant. The people most at risk of this are not the workers who hate their jobs. They are the pastors, the artists, the surgeons, the missionaries — the people whose work is so obviously good that they never suspect it might be an idol.

I have felt this in ministry. The work is holy; the calling is real; and it is exactly the holiness of the work that lets it quietly become the thing I serve. When my worth rises and falls with the size of the crowd or the response to the sermon, I have made the calling into my god, and it is a cruel god, and it will never give me enough.

The Calling of the Unfulfilled

Now to the majority, because most people do not experience their work as calling in the passionate sense, and the self-help gospel has nothing to say to them except that they should quit and find something better, which most of them cannot do. Here the doctrine of vocation offers something the culture cannot: dignity without passion.

The Reformation understanding of vocation never required that you feel called to your work. Luther's milkmaid was not called to milking because milking made her come alive. She was called to it because it was the station God had placed her in, the work through which she served her neighbor and provided for her family, and it was holy for that reason alone. Feelings did not enter into it. A calling, in this understanding, is not a passion you discover but a duty you receive — the actual work in front of you, done faithfully as unto God, whether or not it thrills you.

This is enormously freeing for the person stuck in a job they would not have chosen. Your work is not less of a calling because you do not love it. The single father working two jobs he despises to keep his children fed is living out his calling as truly as any celebrated professional living their dream. More truly, perhaps, because he is doing it without the reward of enjoyment, purely for the love of the ones he serves. That is closer to the cross than any dream job.

Discerning the Secondary Callings

But God does direct people to particular works, and the question of how to discern that direction is a real one, especially for the young and for those at a crossroads. The doctrine of vocation offers wisdom here without offering the false certainty the culture promises. Frederick Buechner's famous line — that vocation is the place where your deep gladness and the world's deep hunger meet — captures part of it, though it is more romantic than the Reformers would have been. Real discernment involves attending to several things at once: your gifts and abilities, the needs around you, the doors God opens and closes, the counsel of wise people who know you, and your own honest desires held loosely before God.

None of these is decisive alone. Your desires can deceive you. Your gifts can be used in many fields. The needs of the world are endless and you cannot meet all of them. The doors that open are not always the right ones. Discernment is not solving an equation; it is the patient, prayerful work of a person who wants God's direction more than their own preference, and who is willing to be surprised. And it is rarely a lightning bolt. Most people discover their calling by walking, not by waiting — by taking faithful next steps and looking back to see the path.

Holding It All Loosely

The final word on calling has to be about holding it loosely, because callings change and end. The person called to raise young children is not called to that forever; the children grow up. The person called to a career gives it up to retirement or has it taken by illness or economic collapse. If your calling is fused with your identity, every ending is a death. But if your primary calling is to God, then the secondary callings can come and go, rise and fall, be given and taken, and you remain — because your worth was never in the work but in the one who called you before you did any work at all.

Find your calling, then. But find the primary one first. Be called to God, belong to Christ, become his — and then receive whatever secondary work he gives you, whether you love it or endure it, as the place he has sent you to serve. That is a calling no economy can take away and no failure can revoke, and it will hold you when every other calling has ended.

The Tyranny of the Dream Job

Our culture has done something cruel to the young in the name of encouragement. It has told them that somewhere out there is a perfect job, a dream career, a calling that will fit them like a glove and make every Monday a joy, and that their task is to find it. This sounds inspiring. It is actually a form of tyranny, because it sets up an impossible standard against which every real job will disappoint, and it produces a generation perpetually restless, perpetually convinced that the meaningful work is elsewhere, perpetually unable to commit to the good work in front of them because it is not the mythical perfect work they were promised.

The doctrine of vocation dismantles this tyranny. It says there is no perfect job, because you are a fallen person working in a fallen world, and every job will involve thorns. It says that calling is not primarily about finding the work that fulfills you but about serving faithfully wherever God has placed you. It frees the young person from the anxious search for the dream and gives them permission to commit — to plant themselves in real work, imperfect and demanding as it is, and to find their meaning not in the perfection of the task but in the faithfulness of the service and the God they serve through it. The dream job is a myth. The faithful life is available to anyone, in almost any work, right now.

When the Calling Changes

One of the most disorienting experiences in the Christian life is the sense that a calling that was once clearly yours is now ending or shifting. The work you were sure God had given you dries up. The passion fades. The doors that were open close, and new ones open toward something you never planned. People often interpret this as failure or as evidence that they misheard God the first time. Usually it is neither. It is simply the nature of secondary callings, which are given for seasons and not forever.

God led Israel through the wilderness by a cloud that moved, and when the cloud moved, they moved, and when it stopped, they stopped. The calling of God is often like that cloud — it settles over a work for a time, and then it lifts and moves on, and the faithful response is not to cling to the place the cloud has left but to follow it to the new place. The person whose identity is fused with a particular calling cannot follow the cloud; they stay camped over an empty spot, grieving a work God has already released them from. But the person whose primary calling is to God himself can follow wherever the cloud leads, holding each secondary calling with open hands, trusting that the God who gave the last work is the one giving the next. Callings change. The Caller does not.

The Hidden Callings

We tend to reserve the language of calling for jobs and careers, but the doctrine of vocation is far broader, and reclaiming its breadth relieves much of the pressure the career-obsessed version creates. You are called not only to your work but to your marriage, your children, your friendships, your neighborhood, your church, the particular people God has placed in your life. These are callings as real as any occupation, and for many people they are the more important ones. The person who pours themselves into a demanding career while neglecting the calling to their spouse and children has not fulfilled their vocation by succeeding at work; they have failed the deeper callings while excelling at the shallower one.

This matters because our culture ranks the callings entirely by their public visibility and economic reward, and the doctrine of vocation refuses that ranking. The father's calling to his children is not less than his calling to his job; it may be greater. The friend's calling to be present in another's suffering is a genuine vocation, though no one pays for it and no resume records it. When you understand that God calls you to a whole life and not merely to a career, the crushing weight of finding the perfect job lifts, because the job is only one of many callings, and often not the most important. A person can have an unremarkable job and a magnificent vocation, faithful in the hidden callings that the world never sees but heaven counts as the substance of a life well lived.

Faithfulness Over Fruitfulness

There is one final correction the doctrine of vocation offers to a culture obsessed with impact, and it is perhaps the most freeing of all. We are taught to measure a calling by its results — the difference it makes, the lives it changes, the mark it leaves. But Scripture measures a calling by faithfulness, not fruitfulness. The servant in the parable is commended not for the size of the return but for being faithful with what was entrusted. The prophet Jeremiah was faithful for decades and saw almost no fruit; by the world's metric of impact, his ministry was a failure. God's verdict was otherwise.

This releases the person whose faithful labor seems to produce little. You may pour yourself into a calling and see no visible result — the parent whose child rebels, the teacher whose students forget, the worker whose good labor goes unrecognized, the servant whose sacrifice changes nothing anyone can measure. In the economy of impact, you have wasted yourself. In the economy of the kingdom, you have been faithful, and faithfulness is the only thing God finally asks. The results belong to him; the faithfulness belongs to you. Find your calling, then, and be faithful in it, and leave the fruit to the God who alone can produce it and who measures your life not by what it accomplished but by whether you were faithful with what he gave you.
